title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: Wald distribution (also known inverse Gaussian distribution) describes first-passage time Wiener process (Brownian motion drift) single absorbing boundary. context decision-making, models time takes evidence accumulate decision threshold. shifted Wald distribution adds non-decision time component account processes like stimulus encoding motor response execution: \[ RT = T_{decision} + T_{ndt} \] \(T_{decision}\) follows Wald distribution \(T_{ndt}\) non-decision time. probability density function shifted Wald : \[ f(t | v, , \tau) = \frac{}{\sqrt{2\pi (t-\tau)^3}} \exp\left(-\frac{(- v(t-\tau))^2}{2(t-\tau)}\right) \] \(t > \tau\), : \(v\) drift rate (rate evidence accumulation) \(\) boundary (decision threshold) \(\tau\) non-decision time

title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: tasks high accuracy, responses correct. “censored” aspect model refers error responses handled. Instead modeling errors arising separate accumulation process toward wrong boundary (full diffusion model), errors treated censored observations — trials correct response yet reached. censoring approach assumes : Correct responses follow shifted Wald distribution Error responses represent trials accumulation process interrupted reaching correct boundary likelihood correct response Wald density: \[ L_{correct}(t) = f_{Wald}(t - \tau | v, ) \] likelihood error response survivor function (1 - CDF): \[ L_{error}(t) = S_{Wald}(t - \tau | v, ) = 1 - F_{Wald}(t - \tau | v, ) \]

what: Generating Simulated Data with Hierarchical Structure
title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: ’ll simulate data multiple participants individual differences drift rates, demonstrating fit hierarchical models bmm: Let’s visualize RT distributions participant:
code: # set seed for reproducibility set.seed(42)  # simulate data for 3 participants in two conditions n_subjects <- 5 n_per_condition <- 200  # fewer trials per condition to keep file size manageable  # Population-level parameters pop_drift_A <- 3.0      # mean drift for condition A pop_drift_B <- 1.8      # mean drift for condition B drift_sd <- 0.5         # between-subject SD in drift bound <- 1.5            # shared boundary ndt <- 0.3              # shared non-decision time  # Generate subject-specific drift rates subject_drifts_A <- rnorm(n_subjects, pop_drift_A, drift_sd) subject_drifts_B <- rnorm(n_subjects, pop_drift_B, drift_sd)  # Simulate data for each subject and condition dat_list <- list() for (i in 1:n_subjects) {   # Condition A   dat_A <- rcswald(n = n_per_condition,                     drift = subject_drifts_A[i],                     bound = bound,                     ndt = ndt)   dat_A$id <- paste0("S", i)   dat_A$condition <- "A"      # Condition B   dat_B <- rcswald(n = n_per_condition,                     drift = subject_drifts_B[i],                     bound = bound,                     ndt = ndt)   dat_B$id <- paste0("S", i)   dat_B$condition <- "B"      dat_list[[2*i-1]] <- dat_A   dat_list[[2*i]] <- dat_B }  # Combine all data dat <- do.call(rbind, dat_list) dat$id <- factor(dat$id) dat$condition <- factor(dat$condition)  # Check error rates by subject and condition error_rates <- aggregate(response ~ id + condition, data = dat,                          FUN = function(x) mean(x == 0)) print(error_rates) #>    id condition response #> 1  S1         A    0.025 #> 2  S2         A    0.020 #> 3  S3         A    0.015 #> 4  S4         A    0.010 #> 5  S5         A    0.020 #> 6  S1         B    0.075 #> 7  S2         B    0.010 #> 8  S3         B    0.130 #> 9  S4         B    0.020 #> 10 S5         B    0.065 ggplot(dat, aes(x = rt, fill = factor(response))) +   geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, position = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +   facet_grid(id ~ condition, labeller = labeller(     condition = c(A = "Condition A", B = "Condition B")   )) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "red", "1" = "blue"),                     labels = c("0" = "Error", "1" = "Correct"),                     name = "Response") +   labs(x = "Response Time (s)", y = "Count",        title = "RT distributions by participant and condition") +   theme_classic()

title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: want estimate: Population-level effects: drift rate varies condition Individual differences: Random effects drift rate participant Shared parameters: Boundary non-decision time constant across participants formula includes fixed effects condition random effects (varying intercepts) participants: (0 + condition | id) term drift formula specifies random slopes condition participant. allows model estimate: population-level drift rate condition Individual deviations population means condition variability (SD) correlation individual differences across conditions hierarchical structure provides several advantages: Partial pooling: Individual estimates pulled toward group mean, providing stable estimates participants less data Uncertainty quantification: model quantifies within- -subject variability Shrinkage: Extreme individual estimates regularized toward group mean
code: formula <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),  # fixed condition effects + random subject effects   bound ~ 1,                          # shared boundary   ndt ~ 1                             # shared non-decision time )

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) one widely used cognitive models analyzing response time (RT) accuracy data two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks. Originally developed Ratcliff (1978), DDM become cornerstone cognitive psychology neuroscience research decision-making processes. DDM ideal : RT data two-choice decision task correct error responses want decompose decision-making separate cognitive processes need account speed-accuracy tradeoffs want model trial--trial variability decision processes ’re interested linking cognitive parameters neural behavioral measures bmm package provides single DDM specification default fixed starting point. include formula zr bmf() call, starting point becomes freely estimated parameter. Trial--Trial variability parameters DDM currently supported, due feasibility Bayesian hierarchical estimation.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM models decision-making noisy accumulation evidence time toward one two decision boundaries. evidence accumulation process described Wiener diffusion process: \[ dX(t) = v \cdot dt + s \cdot dW(t) \] : \(X(t)\) accumulated evidence time \(t\) \(v\) drift rate (average rate evidence accumulation) \(s\) within-trial noise (standard deviation diffusion process, typically fixed 0.1 1) \(dW(t)\) Wiener process (Brownian motion) process starts position \(z \cdot \) (\(z\) starting point parameter \(\) boundary separation) continues reaches one two absorbing boundaries 0 (lower/incorrect) \(\) (upper/correct).

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Typical range: -5 5 (task-dependent) Interpretation: Quality evidence, task difficulty, attention Typical range: 0.5 3 Interpretation: Response caution, speed-accuracy tradeoff Typical range: 0.1 0.5 seconds Interpretation: Perceptual motor latencies

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Starting point bias (\(z_r\)): Relative starting point evidence accumulation (0 = lower boundary, 1 = upper boundary). Default: fixed 0 (implies \(z_r = 0.5\) response scale) Interpretation: priori response bias

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: full DDM, described Ratcliff McKoon (2008) implemented Henrich et al. (2024) STAN, includes three additional parameters capture trial--trial variability core parameters: Drift rate variability (\(s_v\) sdrift): -trial variability drift rate, accounting fluctuations evidence quality across trials (typical range: 0 2). Non-decision time variability (\(s_{t_0}\) sndt): -trial variability non-decision time, accounting variable encoding/motor times (typical range: 0 0.2). Starting point variability (\(s_z\) szr): -trial variability starting point, accounting variable response bias across trials (typical range: 0 0.5). 7-parameter version implemented bmm: variability parameters theoretically important can improve model fit, Henrich et al. (2024) demonstrated 7-parameter likelihood prohibitively long computation times, especially hierarchical Bayesian estimation. Key limitations include: Single-subject feasibility : Even 100-300 trials, model fitting can 20 minutes using within-chain parallelization. 1500+ trials typical robust DDM estimation, runtimes likely extend hours even days. Hierarchical models infeasible: common use case cognitive research (multiple subjects, conditions, trials) becomes computationally intractable without high-performance computing resources. typical hierarchical study (20+ subjects, 2-3 conditions, 200+ trials per condition) likely require weeks computation time. Limited practical benefit: research questions, fixed- free-starting-point models provide adequate fits interpretable parameters, making substantial computational cost 7-parameter version difficult justify. researchers specifically interested trial--trial variability parameters, recommend considering simulation-based inference methods (e.g., BayesFlow) fitting separate single-subject models rather hierarchical approaches.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM predicts complete RT distributions correct error responses, including: Mean RT accuracy RT variability (standard deviation) Shape RT distributions (skewness, leading edge) Speed-accuracy tradeoffs Effects experimental manipulations different cognitive processes

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM likelihood requires numerical solution Fokker-Planck equation, can computationally demanding large datasets. Runtime scales approximately linearly number trials. typical datasets (100-300 trials), models fit quickly (< 20 seconds modern hardware 4 chains × 2000 iterations). Larger datasets (1500+ trials) may take several minutes single-subject models several hours hierarchical models many subjects. Practical recommendations: Start default model (fixed zr) test model specification. Use default cores = 4 parallelize chains efficiently. hierarchical models, consider starting random intercepts adding random slopes. Test subset data first verify model specification estimate total runtime.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: rr98 dataset rtdists package provides classic example choice response time data. dataset contains responses brightness discrimination task participants judged whether pixel arrays “high” “low” brightness. dataset includes: rt: Response time seconds response_num: Binary response (1 = “dark”, 2 = “light”) instruction: Speed vs accuracy emphasis strength: Task difficulty (0-32, brightness level) id: Participant identifier dataset ideal DDM analysis : Sufficient error trials: Unlike tasks near-ceiling accuracy Multiple conditions: Speed vs accuracy emphasis Clear manipulation: Brightness strength affects evidence quality Rich structure: Individual differences trial-level variability
code: library(bmm) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr)  # Load the dataset from rtdists data(rr98, package = "rtdists")  # Remove outliers as in the original analysis rr98 <- rr98[!rr98$outlier, ]  # Examine structure str(rr98[, c("id", "rt", "response_num", "instruction", "strength")])  # Check accuracy by condition rr98 %>%   mutate(correct = (response_num == 1 & strength <= 16) |                     (response_num == 2 & strength > 16)) %>%   group_by(id, instruction) %>%   summarise(accuracy = mean(correct), .groups = "drop")

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM requires: numeric RT variable (positive values) binary response variable coded 0/1 “lower”/“upper”
code: # Prepare data for DDM analysis # Focus on one participant and instruction condition for demonstration demo_data <- rr98 %>%   dplyr::filter(id == "jf", instruction == "accuracy") %>%   mutate(     # Recode response: 1 = "upper", 0 = "lower"     response = ifelse(response_num == 1, 0, 1)   )  # Check response coding table(demo_data$response)  # Visualize RT distributions by response ggplot(demo_data, aes(x = rt, fill = factor(response))) +   facet_wrap(~ strength) +   geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, bins = 30, position = "identity") +   labs(x = "Response Time (s)", y = "Count", fill = "Response") +   theme_minimal()

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: simplest DDM drift, boundary, non-decision time: Interpreting fixed-zr model: drift: Higher values indicate faster evidence accumulation (easier trials) bound: Higher values indicate cautious responding ndt: Time spent non-decision processes
code: # Define the model model_fixed_zr <- ddm(rt = "rt",                        response = "response")  # Define the formula - let drift vary by strength formula_fixed_zr <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength,   bound ~ 1,   ndt ~ 1 )  # Fit the model  fit_fixed_zr <- bmm(   formula = formula_fixed_zr,   data = demo_data,   model = model_fixed_zr,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4,   chains = 4,   iter = 2000,   warmup = 1000,   file = "assets/bmmfit_ddm_fixed_zr_vignette" )  # Examine convergence summary(fit_fixed_zr)  # Check diagnostics plot(fit_fixed_zr)

what: DDM with Free Starting Point Bias
title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Adding starting point bias allows modeling priori response preferences: use starting point bias: suspect priori response preferences conditions systematically favor one response testing theoretical predictions response bias
code: # Define the model with free `zr` model_free_zr <- ddm(rt = "rt",                       response = "response")  # Define the formula formula_free_zr <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength,   bound ~ 1,   ndt ~ 1,   zr ~ 1  # starting point bias )  # Fit the model fit_free_zr <- bmm(   formula = formula_free_zr,   data = demo_data,   model = model_free_zr,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4,   file = "assets/bmmfit_ddm_free_zr_vignette" )  # Compare models loo_fixed_zr <- loo(fit_fixed_zr) loo_free_zr <- loo(fit_free_zr) loo_compare(loo_fixed_zr, loo_free_zr)

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: One key advantages fitting DDMs Bayesian framework bmm ability easily specify hierarchical models account individual differences.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Benefits hierarchical modeling: Partial pooling: Borrows strength across subjects better estimates Individual differences: Quantifies -subject variability Handles unbalanced data: Works even different trial counts per subject Shrinkage: Extreme individual estimates pulled toward group mean
code: # Use multiple subjects from rr98 multi_subject_data <- rr98 %>%   filter(instruction == "accuracy") %>%   mutate(response = ifelse(response_num == 1, 0, 1)) %>%   select(id, rt, response, strength)  # Hierarchical model model_hier <- ddm(rt = "rt",                    response = "response")  # Formula with random effects formula_hier <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength + (0 + strength | id),   bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),   ndt ~ 1 + (1 | id) )  # Fit hierarchical model fit_hier <- bmm(   formula = formula_hier,   data = multi_subject_data,   model = model_hier,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4 )  # Extract individual-level parameters # This gives you person-specific drift, bound, and ndt estimates

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Test experimental manipulations affect different cognitive processes: Theoretical predictions: Speed emphasis: Lower boundary (faster, less accurate) Accuracy emphasis: Higher boundary (slower, accurate) Drift: primarily reflect stimulus strength, instruction
code: # Compare speed vs accuracy emphasis full_data <- rr98 %>%   mutate(response = ifelse(response_num == 1, 0, 1)) %>%   select(id, rt, response, instruction, strength)  # Model with instruction effects formula_instruction <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength + (0 + strength | id),   bound ~ instruction + (instruction | id),   ndt ~ 1 + (1 | id) )  fit_instruction <- bmm(   formula = formula_instruction,   data = full_data,   model = model_hier,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4 )

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Use information criteria compare model fit: General findings (simulation studies): Fixed-zr model often sufficient applications Free-zr model improves fit response bias present Model selection balance fit quality interpretability
code: # Compute LOO for each model loo_fixed_zr <- loo(fit_fixed_zr) loo_free_zr <- loo(fit_free_zr)  # Compare models loo_compare(loo_fixed_zr, loo_free_zr)  # Check for influential observations plot(loo_free_zr)

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM joint model response times responses, adequate model reproduce . pp_check() checks RT distribution default; resp_var argument selects observables likelihood (see pp_check_vars(fit) options):
code: # Default: the RT distribution pp_check(fit_fixed_zr)  # The response distribution (choice proportions) pp_check(fit_fixed_zr, resp_var = "response")  # RTs signed by the response (lower-boundary RTs negative), so the # speed *and* frequency of errors are checked in one display pp_check(fit_fixed_zr, resp_var = "signed_rt")  # All checks as a panel, drawn from one shared joint simulation pp_check(fit_fixed_zr, resp_var = "all")  # Facet any check by a predictor of the fitted model pp_check(fit_instruction, resp_var = "signed_rt", group = "instruction")  # Quantile-probability plots (QP plots) # These are the gold standard for evaluating DDM fits # Shows predicted vs observed RT quantiles for correct/error responses

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: default, bmm uses appropriate link functions: drift: identity (can positive negative) bound: log (must positive) ndt: log (must positive) zr: logit (must 0 1) sdrift, sndt: log (must positive) szr: logit (must 0 1) can customize links needed:
code: # Use log link for drift (forces positive values) model_custom_links <- ddm(   rt = "rt",   response = "response",   links = list(drift = "log") )

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM advantages: Models correct error responses Accounts response bias variability Richer theoretical interpretation Standard field cswald advantages: Much faster fit (minutes vs hours) Simpler interpretation fewer parameters Adequate high-accuracy tasks stable small samples Recommendation: Use cswald initial exploration errors rare (<10%); use DDM complete analysis computational resources allow.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Based simulation studies practical experience: Minimum: 50 trials per condition (fixed zr) Adequate: 100-200 trials per condition (free zr) Recommended: 200+ trials per condition stable estimates Hierarchical models: least 5-10 subjects per group

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Always check: Rhat < 1.01 parameters (indicates chain convergence) ESS > 400 (effective sample size, indicates sufficient sampling) divergent transitions (indicates numerical issues) Trace plots look like “hairy caterpillars” Posterior predictive checks show good fit

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Problem: Divergent transitions - Solution: Increase adapt_delta (e.g., 0.95 0.99) Problem: Slow mixing / low ESS - Solution: Increase iterations, use informative priors, check reparameterization Problem: Boundary estimates extremes - Solution: Check data quality, consider informative priors Problem: Non-decision time longer minimum RT - Solution: Check fast outliers, consider data trimming Problem: Starting point estimates 0 1 - Solution: May indicate model misspecification insufficient data

text: Stan code used fitting model generated together bmm brms. bmm takes care code specific model, brms generates code regression syntax, priors everything else. want get Stan code used fitting model, can inspect modify , can use stancode() function brms: Alternatively, already fitted model object, can just call stancode() object, give result:
code: stancode(bmf(c ~ 0 + set_size, kappa ~ 0 + set_size),           data = oberauer_lin_2017,          model = sdm(resp_error = 'dev_rad')) // generated with brms 2.23.0 and bmm 1.3.2.9000 functions {   /* compute the tan_half link    * Args:    *   x: a scalar in (-pi, pi)    * Returns:    *   a scalar in (-Inf, Inf)    */    real tan_half(real x) {      return tan(x / 2);    }   /* compute the tan_half link (vectorized)    * Args:    *   x: a vector in (-pi, pi)    * Returns:    *   a vector in (-Inf, Inf)    */    vector tan_half(vector x) {      return tan(x / 2);    }   /* compute the inverse of the tan_half link    * Args:    *   y: a scalar in (-Inf, Inf)    * Returns:    *   a scalar in (-pi, pi)    */    real inv_tan_half(real y) {      return 2 * atan(y);    }   /* compute the inverse of the tan_half link (vectorized)    * Args:    *   y: a vector in (-Inf, Inf)    * Returns:    *   a vector in (-pi, pi)    */    vector inv_tan_half(vector y) {      return 2 * atan(y);    }      // utility function trick for converting real to integer type   int bin_search(real x, int min_val, int max_val) {       int mid_p;       int L = min_val;       int R = max_val;       while(L < R) {         mid_p = (R-L) %/% 2;         if (L + mid_p < x) {           L += mid_p + 1;         } else if (L + mid_p > x) {           R = L + mid_p - 1;         } else {           return(L + mid_p);         }       }       return(L);     }    // utility function for determining optimal number of chebyshev points for the denominator approximation   int get_m(real c, real kappa) {     real m = floor(2 * exp(0.4*c) * kappa^(fma(c,0.0145,0.7)) + 0.5)+2;     int M = bin_search(m, 2, 200);     return(M);   }    // log of the numerator of the sdm likelihood   real sdm_simple_lpdf(vector y, vector mu, vector c, vector kappa) {     int N = size(y);     vector[N] num = exp(fma(kappa,cos(y-mu)-1,c)) ;     real out = dot_product(num, sqrt(kappa));     out *= inv(sqrt2()) * inv_sqrt(pi());     return(out);   }    // log of the normalization constant, approximated by chebyshev quadrature   real sdm_simple_ldenom_chquad_adaptive(real c, real kappa, matrix CN) {     int m = get_m(c,kappa);     vector[m] cosn = CN[1:m,m];     vector[m] fn = exp(fma(kappa,cosn,c)) * sqrt(kappa) * inv(sqrt2()) * inv_sqrt(pi());     real out = -log_sum_exp(fn)+log(m);     return(out);   }    real sdm_simple_run_ldenom(vector c, vector kappa, matrix CN,                              int G_runs, array[] int run_start,                              array[] int run_count) {     real out = 0;     for (g in 1:G_runs) {       int n = run_start[g];       real z = sdm_simple_ldenom_chquad_adaptive(c[n], kappa[n], CN);       out += run_count[g] * z;     }     return(out);   }    real sdm_simple_run_ldenom_slice(vector c, vector kappa, matrix CN,                                    int start, int end, int G_runs,                                    array[] int run_start,                                    array[] int run_count) {     real out = 0;     for (g in 1:G_runs) {       if (run_start[g] >= start && run_start[g] <= end) {         int n = run_start[g] - start + 1;         real z = sdm_simple_ldenom_chquad_adaptive(c[n], kappa[n], CN);         out += run_count[g] * z;       }     }     return(out);   } } data {   int<lower=1> N;  // total number of observations   vector[N] Y;  // response variable   int<lower=1> K_c;  // number of population-level effects   matrix[N, K_c] X_c;  // population-level design matrix   int<lower=1> K_kappa;  // number of population-level effects   matrix[N, K_kappa] X_kappa;  // population-level design matrix   int prior_only;  // should the likelihood be ignored?   int G_sdm_runs;   array[G_sdm_runs] int sdm_run_start;   array[G_sdm_runs] int sdm_run_count; } transformed data {     // precompute chebyshev points   matrix[200,200] COSN;   for (m in 1:200) {     for (i in 1:m) {       COSN[i,m] = cos((2*i-1)*pi()/(2*m))-1;     }   }   // fail fast if the precomputed run metadata does not describe the data Stan   // received (it is computed in R and can drift out of sync with the data)   {     int sdm_run_total = 0;     for (g in 1:G_sdm_runs) {       if (sdm_run_start[g] < 1 || sdm_run_start[g] > N) {         reject("bmm error: sdm_run_start[", g, "] = ", sdm_run_start[g],                " is outside the data range [1, ", N, "]. The SDM run metadata ",                "does not match the model data. Please report this at ",                "https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm/issues");       }       if (g > 1 && sdm_run_start[g] <= sdm_run_start[g - 1]) {         reject("bmm error: sdm_run_start must be strictly increasing. The SDM ",                "run metadata does not match the model data. Please report ",                "this at https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm/issues");       }       sdm_run_total += sdm_run_count[g];     }     if (sdm_run_total != N) {       reject("bmm error: sum(sdm_run_count) = ", sdm_run_total, " but N = ", N,              ". The SDM run metadata does not match the model data. Please ",              "report this at https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm/issues");     }   } } parameters {   vector[K_c] b_c;  // regression coefficients   vector[K_kappa] b_kappa;  // regression coefficients } transformed parameters {   real Intercept;  // temporary intercept for centered predictors   // prior contributions to the log posterior   real lprior = 0;   Intercept = 0;   lprior += student_t_lpdf(b_c | 5, 2, 0.75);   lprior += student_t_lpdf(b_kappa | 5, 1.75, 0.75); } model {   // likelihood including constants   if (!prior_only) {     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] mu = rep_vector(0.0, N);     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] c = rep_vector(0.0, N);     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] kappa = rep_vector(0.0, N);     mu += Intercept;     c += X_c * b_c;     kappa += X_kappa * b_kappa;     mu = inv_tan_half(mu);     kappa = exp(kappa);     target += sdm_simple_lpdf(Y | mu, c, kappa);       target += sdm_simple_run_ldenom(c, kappa, COSN, G_sdm_runs,                                     sdm_run_start, sdm_run_count);     target += -(log2()+log(pi()))*N;   }   // priors including constants   target += lprior; } generated quantities {   // actual population-level intercept   real b_Intercept = Intercept; } fit <- bmm(bmf(c ~ 0 + set_size, kappa ~ 0 + set_size),                data = oberauer_lin_2017,               model = sdm(resp_error = 'dev_rad')) stancode(fit)

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: diffusion model (Ratcliff 1978) widely used model speeded decision-making. describes participants accumulate noisy evidence time reaching one two decision boundaries. Usually, diffusion model fit trial-level reaction time distributions, can computationally intensive, especially hierarchical Bayesian estimation. EZ-Diffusion Model (Wagenmakers et al. 2007) provides simplified alternative building closed-form equations relate parameters diffusion model easily computed summary statistics: mean reaction time (MRT), reaction time variance (VRT), accuracy (proportion correct, Pc). makes possible calculate diffusion model parameters aggregated data without fitting individual trials.

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: standard diffusion model, evidence accumulates starting point toward one two boundaries. key parameters : Drift rate (\(v\)): average rate evidence accumulation, reflecting task difficulty ability Boundary separation (\(\)): distance two decision boundaries, reflecting speed-accuracy tradeoff Non-decision time (\(T_{er}\)): Time processes outside decision (encoding, motor response) Starting point (\(z\)): response bias indicating evidence accumulation begins relative boundaries Figure 1.1: Illustration diffusion model. Evidence accumulates starting point reaching upper (correct) lower (error) boundary.

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: Wagenmakers et al. (2007) provided closed-form solutions relating diffusion model parameters observable summary statistics. 3-parameter version (assuming symmetric starting point, \(z = /2\)): Given proportion correct (\(P_c\)), mean RT correct responses (\(MRT\)), variance correct RTs (\(VRT\)), parameters can computed : \[ v = \text{sign}(P_c - 0.5) \cdot s \cdot \left[ L(P_c) \cdot \frac{P_c^2 L(P_c) - P_c \cdot L(P_c) + P_c - 0.5}{VRT} \right]^{1/4} \] \[ = s^2 \cdot \frac{L(P_c)}{v} \] \[ T_{er} = MRT - \frac{}{2v} \cdot \frac{1 - e^{-\frac{va}{s^2}}}{1 + e^{-\frac{va}{s^2}}} \] \(L(P_c) = \ln\left(\frac{P_c}{1 - P_c}\right)\) logit function \(s\) diffusion constant (typically fixed 1 identification).

code: library(bmm) library(rtdists) library(dplyr)  set.seed(42)  # Generate clean trial-level data with known parameters n_trials <- 200 true_drift <- 2.5 true_bound <- 1.2 true_ndt <- 0.25  # Simulate diffusion process trials_clean <- rdiffusion(   n = n_trials,   a = true_bound,   v = true_drift,   t0 = true_ndt,   z = 0.5 * true_bound )  # Add contaminants (5% fast guesses and lapses) n_contaminants <- round(n_trials * 0.05) contaminant_idx <- sample(n_trials, n_contaminants)  trials_contaminated <- trials_clean trials_contaminated$rt[contaminant_idx] <- runif(n_contaminants, 0.1, 3) trials_contaminated$response[contaminant_idx] <- sample(c("upper", "lower"),                                                          n_contaminants,                                                          replace = TRUE)  trials_contaminated <- trials_contaminated |>   mutate(     correct = as.numeric(response == "upper"),     subject = 1,     condition = "standard"   ) summary_simple <- ezdm_summary_stats(   trials_contaminated$rt, trials_contaminated$correct,   method = "simple", version = "3par" )  summary_robust <- ezdm_summary_stats(   trials_contaminated$rt, trials_contaminated$correct,   method = "robust", version = "3par" )  summary_mixture <- ezdm_summary_stats(   trials_contaminated$rt, trials_contaminated$correct,   method = "mixture", version = "3par" )  comparison <- data.frame(   Method = c("Simple", "Robust", "Mixture", "TRUE"),   Mean_RT = c(     summary_simple$mean_rt,     summary_robust$mean_rt,     summary_mixture$mean_rt,     mean(trials_clean$rt[trials_clean$response == "upper"])   ),   Var_RT = c(     summary_simple$var_rt,     summary_robust$var_rt,     summary_mixture$var_rt,     var(trials_clean$rt[trials_clean$response == "upper"])   ),   Contaminant = c(NA, NA, summary_mixture$contaminant_prop, 0.05) )  print(comparison) #>    Method   Mean_RT     Var_RT Contaminant #> 1  Simple 0.5409176 0.10605857          NA #> 2  Robust 0.4568634 0.02440439          NA #> 3 Mixture 0.4962307 0.03633472  0.03539257 #> 4    TRUE 0.4755037 0.02050638  0.05000000

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)

code: set.seed(123)  # Define true parameters for two conditions true_params <- data.frame(   condition = c("easy", "hard"),   drift = c(3.0, 1.5),   bound = c(1.5, 1.5),   ndt = c(0.3, 0.3) )  # Number of subjects and trials per condition n_subjects <- 20 n_trials <- 100  # Generate data sim_data <- data.frame() for (subj in 1:n_subjects) {   for (cond in 1:2) {     # Add some random variation for each subject     drift_subj <- true_params$drift[cond] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.3)     bound_subj <- true_params$bound[cond] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.1)     ndt_subj <- true_params$ndt[cond] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.02)      # Generate summary statistics     stats <- rezdm(       n = 1,       n_trials = n_trials,       drift = max(drift_subj, 0.1),       bound = max(bound_subj, 0.5),       ndt = max(ndt_subj, 0.1),       version = "3par"     )      stats$subject <- subj     stats$condition <- true_params$condition[cond]     sim_data <- rbind(sim_data, stats)   } }  # Convert condition to factor sim_data$condition <- factor(sim_data$condition, levels = c("easy", "hard"))  head(sim_data) #>     mean_rt     var_rt n_upper n_trials subject condition #> 1 0.5849755 0.02704076      96      100       1      easy #> 2 0.7349579 0.05481245      89      100       1      hard #> 3 0.5064378 0.01015706     100      100       2      easy #> 4 0.6327151 0.07406956      91      100       2      hard #> 5 0.5354869 0.01897598      98      100       3      easy #> 6 0.6624182 0.07254991      85      100       3      hard

code: # set seed for reproducibility set.seed(123)  # specfiy generating parameters Cs <- c(4,4,2,2) As <- c(0.5,1,0.5,0.5) Ss <- c(10,10,5,5) kappas <- c(15,10,15,10) nTrials = 2000 set_size = 5  simData <- data.frame() for (i in 1:length(Cs)) {   # generate different non-target locations for each condition   item_location <- c(0, runif(set_size - 1, -pi,pi))      # generate different distances for each condition   item_distance <- c(0, runif(set_size - 1, min = 0.1, max = pi))      # simulate data for each condition   genData <- rimm(n = nTrials,                   mu = item_location,                   dist = item_distance,                   c = Cs[i], a = As[i],                   b = 1, s = Ss[i], kappa = kappas[i])      condData <- data.frame(     resp_error = genData,     trialID = 1:nTrials,     cond = i,     color_item1 = 0,     dist_item1 = 0   )      init_colnames <- colnames(condData)      for (j in 1:(set_size - 1)) {     condData <- cbind(condData,item_location[j + 1])     condData <- cbind(condData,item_distance[j + 1])   }      colnames(condData) <- c(init_colnames,                           paste0(rep(c("color_item","dist_item"),times = set_size - 1),                                   rep(2:(set_size),each = 2)))      simData <- rbind(simData,condData) }  # convert condition variable to a factor  simData$cond <- as.factor(simData$cond)

text: control visualization, can obtain posterior predictions directly using tidybayes package build custom plot.
code: library(tidybayes) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2)  pp_m3 <- m3_fit |>   # obtain expected predicted draws   tidybayes::epred_draws(     newdata = m3_fit$data   ) |> ungroup() |>   # select only relevant variables   select(ID, cond, nTrials, .draw, .category, .epred) |>   # calculate the mean predicted values in each condition for each response category   # and each draw   summarise(.epred = mean(.epred/nTrials),             .by = c(cond, .category, .draw))  # reshape data to match the format of the posterior predictives data$n_trials <- rowSums(data[,c("corr","other","dist","npl")], na.rm = T) data_pp <- data |>   select(ID, n_trials, cond, corr, other, dist, npl) |>   tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(corr, other, dist, npl), names_to = ".category", values_to = ".value") |>   mutate(.value = .value/n_trials)  # some responses were not possible in some conditions, so we set them to zero data_pp[is.na(data_pp)] <- 0  # relabel condition factor for better readability levels(pp_m3$cond) <- c("new", "old shuffled", "old same") levels(data_pp$cond) <- c("new", "old shuffled", "old same")  # plot the posterior predictive draws against the observed data ggplot(data = pp_m3,        aes(condition, y = .epred, x = cond, fill = cond)) +   facet_wrap(~.category, scales = "free") +   geom_violin() +   stat_summary(data = data_pp, aes (y = .value),                fun.data = mean_se, size = 0.1) +   labs(y = "Response proportions",        x = "Condition",        fill = "Condition",        title = "Model Fit",        subtitle = "Posterior Predictive vs. Observed Response Proportions")

title: Mixture models for visual working memory
text: two-parameter mixture model (Zhang Luck 2008) three-parameter mixture model (Bays et al. 2009) measurement models continuous reproduction tasks visual working memory domain (details task, see online article. measurement models continuous reproduction tasks, goal model distribution angular response errors. two-parameter mixture model (?mixture2p) distinguishes two memory states lead responses mixture two different distributions angular errors. two states : representation cued object certain precision feature visual working memory (solid blue distribution Figure 1.1) representation visual working memory thus guessing random response (dashed red distribution). Figure 1.1: Mixtures response distributions Responses based noisy memory representation correct feature come circular normal distribution (.e., von Mises) centered correct feature value, guessing responses come uniform distribution along entire circle: \[ p(\theta) = p_{mem} \cdot \text{vM}(\theta; \mu, \kappa) + (1-p_{mem}) \cdot \text{Uniform}(\theta; -\pi, \pi) \\ \] \[ p_{guess} = 1-p_{mem} \\ \] \[ vM(\theta; \mu, \kappa) = \frac{e^{\kappa \cos(\theta - \mu)}}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)} \] \(\theta\) response angle, \(p_{mem}\) probability responses come memory target feature, \(\mu\) mean von Mises distribution representing target feature, \(\kappa\) concentration parameter von Mises distribution, representing precision target memory representation. three-parameter mixture model (?mixture3p) adds third state: confusing cued object another object shown encoding thus reporting feature object (long dashed green distribution Figure 1.1). Responses state sometimes called non-target responses swap errors. non-target responses also come von Mises distribution centered feature non-target object. probability non-target responses represented parameter \(p_{nt}\), complete model : \[ p(\theta) = p_{mem} \cdot \text{vM}(\theta; \mu_t, \kappa) + p_{nt} \cdot \frac{\sum_{=1}^{n} \text{vM}(\theta; \mu_{}, \kappa)}{n} + (1-p_{mem}-p_{nt}) \cdot \text{Uniform}(\theta; -\pi, \pi) \\ \] \[ p_{guess} = 1-p_{mem}-p_{nt} \] \(\mu_{t}\) location target feature, \(\mu_{}\) location -th non-target feature, \(n\) number non-target features. applications model, responses coded angular error relative target feature. true non-target memory representations, assumed centered target feature, precision non-target memory representation assumed precision target memory representation. version model implemented bmm package: \[ p(\theta) = p_{mem} \cdot \text{vM}(\theta; 0, \kappa) + p_{nt} \cdot \frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}  \text{vM}(\theta; \mu_{}-\mu_t, \kappa)}{n} + (1-p_{mem}-p_{nt}) \cdot \text{Uniform}(\theta; -\pi, \pi) \]

text: fit two-parameter mixture model, need specify model formula model. model formula use brms package’s bf function. linear model formulas brms, left side equation refers -predicted variable parameter right side specifies variables used predict . example, want fit model probability memory responses precision memory responses vary set size. also want effect set size vary across participants. model formula three components: response variable error predicted constant term, internally fixed mean 0 precision parameter kappa predicted set size, effect set size varies across participants mixture weight1 memory responses thetat predicted set size, effect set size varies across participants. specify model simply : Finally, fit model bmm() function. fit model function uses brms package fit model, can pass argument pass brm function.
code: ff <- bmf(thetat ~ 0 + set_size + (0 + set_size | id),           kappa ~ 0 + set_size + (0 + set_size | id)) model <- mixture2p(resp_error = "error") fit <- bmm(   formula = ff,   data = dat_preprocessed,   model = model,   cores = 4,   refresh = 100,   backend = 'cmdstanr',   file = "assets/bmmfit_mixture2p_vignette" )

title: Handling RT Contamination in Evidence Accumulation Models
text: Evidence accumulation models assume observed RTs arise single cognitive process. practice, trials reflect something else entirely: anticipatory responses, attention lapses, accidental button presses. Even contaminant trials can bias parameter estimates distort model fit (Ratcliff Tuerlinckx 2002). bmm package provides two functions dealing contamination, one type model supports: fit mixture model via EM algorithm, separating cognitive RTs uniform contaminant distribution (Ratcliff Tuerlinckx 2002): \[ f(RT) = (1 - \pi) \cdot f_{\text{cognitive}}(RT) + \pi \cdot f_{\text{uniform}}(RT) \] \(\pi\) contamination proportion. cognitive component \(f_{\text{cognitive}}\) can ex-Gaussian (default), log-normal, inverse Gaussian. background EZ diffusion model, see Wagenmakers et al. (2007) Wagenmakers et al. (2008); full diffusion model, see Ratcliff McKoon (2008).

First show ezdm_summary_stats() method options work single participant’s data accuracy instruction condition data. histogram shows long tail slow RTs, likely contaminants:  mixture method also returns contamination proportion estimate. robust method faster makes distributional assumptions, quantify contamination.
code: data(rr98)  rr98_subset <- rr98 |>   filter(id == "jf", instruction == "accuracy") |>   mutate(response = ifelse(response == "dark", "upper", "lower")) |>   select(rt, response, strength, correct)  ggplot(rr98_subset, aes(x = rt)) +   geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +   labs(title = "RT Distribution (Ratcliff & Rouder, 1998)",        subtitle = "One participant, accuracy condition",        x = "Response Time (s)", y = "Count") stats_simple <- ezdm_summary_stats(   rr98_subset$rt, rr98_subset$response, method = "simple" ) stats_robust <- ezdm_summary_stats(   rr98_subset$rt, rr98_subset$response, method = "robust" ) stats_mixture <- ezdm_summary_stats(   rr98_subset$rt, rr98_subset$response,   method = "mixture" )  bind_rows(   stats_simple |> mutate(method = "simple"),   stats_robust |> mutate(method = "robust"),   stats_mixture |> mutate(method = "mixture") ) |>   mutate(accuracy = n_upper / n_trials) |>   select(method, mean_rt, var_rt, accuracy, contaminant_prop) #>       method   mean_rt     var_rt  accuracy contaminant_prop #> ...1  simple 0.8231905 0.39684254 0.4752726               NA #> ...2  robust 0.6440000 0.05804206 0.4752726               NA #> mu   mixture 0.7500098 0.11366415 0.4745630       0.02797548

title: Handling RT Contamination in Evidence Accumulation Models
text: simplest approach hard threshold: remove trials \(P(\text{contaminant} \mid RT) > 0.5\). Alternatively, can probabilistically sample removal decisions proportional trial’s contamination probability binomial distribution, avoids sharp cutoff:
code: clean_data <- my_data |>   mutate(contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(rt)) |>   filter(contam_prob <= 0.5) set.seed(123) clean_data <- my_data |>   mutate(contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(rt)) |>   filter(rbinom(n(), 1, contam_prob) == 0)

title: Handling RT Contamination in Evidence Accumulation Models
text: full analysis, flag contaminated trials first, either filter weight fitting DDM csWald. example shows simple filtering workflow:
code: # Step 1: Flag contaminated trials flagged_data <- raw_data |>   group_by(subject, condition) |>   mutate(contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(rt)) |>   ungroup()  # Step 2: Filter clean_data <- flagged_data |> filter(contam_prob < 0.5)  # Step 3: Fit model fit <- bmm(   formula = bmf(drift ~ condition, bound ~ 1, ndt ~ 1),   data = clean_data,   model = ddm(resp1 = "rt", resp2 = "response") )

title: The Signal Discrimination Model (SDM)
text: Signal Discrimination Model measurement model continuous reproduction tasks visual working memory domain. model originally introduced Oberauer (2023). measurement models continuous reproduction tasks, goal model distribution angular response errors. model assumes test probe appears, possible responses circle (\(\theta\)) activated strength depends distance feature stored memory (\(\mu\)) response options. Formally, given following activation function: \[ S(\theta) = c \cdot \frac{\exp(\kappa \cdot \cos(\theta-\mu))}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)} \] \(c\) memory strength parameter, \(\kappa\) precision parameter, \(I_0\) modified Bessel function first kind order 0. Thus, activation function follows von Mises distribution, weigthed memory strength parameter. activation response options corrupted noise, assumed follow Gumbel distribution. response option highest activation value: \[ Pr(\theta) = argmax(S(\theta) + \epsilon) \\ \epsilon \sim Gumbel(0,1) \] equivalent following softmax function (also known exponentiated Luce’s choice rule): \[ Pr(\theta) = \frac{\exp(S(\theta)}{\sum_{=1}^{n} \exp(S(\theta_i))} \] n number response options, often 360 typical visual working memory experiments. summary, model assumes response errors come following distribution, \(\mu = 0\): \[ \Large{f(\theta\ |\ \mu,c,\kappa) = \frac{e^ {c \ \frac{e^{k\ cos(\theta-\mu)}}{2\pi I_o(k)}}}{Z}} \] Z normalizing constant ensure probability mass sums 1.

title: The Signal Discrimination Model (SDM)
text: bmm package use different parametrization. parametrization chosen numerical stability efficiency. Three features parametrization make difficult work practice. First, modified bessel function \(I_0\) increases rapidly, often leading numerical overflow. Second, bessel function expensive compute, estimating model MCMC methods can slow. Third, normalizing constant denominator requires summing 360 terms, also slow. address issues, use following parametrization SDM distribution: \[ \Large{f(\theta\ |\ \mu,c,\kappa) = \frac{ e^{c \ \sqrt{\frac{k}{2\pi}} e^{k \ (cos(\theta-\mu)-1)}} }{Z}} \] parametrization derived known approximation modified bessel function large \(k\) (Abramowitz et al. (1988)): \[ I_0(\kappa) \sim ~ \frac{e^{\kappa}}{\sqrt{2\pi \kappa}}, \ \ \ \ \kappa \rightarrow \infty \] needed, \(c\) parameter original formulation Oberauer (2023) can computed : \[ c_{oberauer} = c_{bmm} \ e^{-\kappa} I_0(\kappa)\sqrt{2 \pi \kappa} \] parametrization change predicted shape distribution, produces slightly different values \(c\) small values \(kappa\). parametrization default bmm package. second optimization concerns calculation normalizing constant \(Z\). original model assumed responses can one 360 discrete values, resulting probability mass function. bmm treat response variable continuous, makes \(f(\theta)\) probability density function. means can calculate normalizing constant \(Z\) integrating \(f(\theta)\) entire circle: \[ Z = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(\theta) d\theta \] integral expressed closed form, can approximated using numerical integration methods. results discrete continuous formulations nearly identical, large number response options (typical applications), number response options small, example 4-AFC tasks.

text: main function fitting models bmm(). function main entry point users fit models. set-independent specific models implemented package. calls several subroutines, implemented generic S3 methods, : configure_options() - configure local options fitting, parallel sampling, check_model() - check model exists check_formula() - check formula specified correctly transform brmsformula check_data() - check whether data contains necessary information configure_model() - configures model called fitting configure_prior() - sets default priors model combines user prior call_brm() - fit model using brm() function brms package postprocess_brm() - post-process fitted model addition, also tests specified bmmodel already estimated saved file. done via read_bmmfit save_bmmfit functions.
code: bmm <- function(formula, data, model,                 prior = NULL,                 sort_data = getOption('bmm.sort_data', "check"),                 silent = getOption('bmm.silent', 1),                 backend = getOption('brms.backend', NULL),                 file = NULL, file_compress = TRUE,                 file_refit = getOption('bmm.file_refit', FALSE), ...) {   deprecated_args(...)   dots <- list(...)    x <- read_bmmfit(file, file_refit)   if (!is.null(x)) return(x)    # set temporary global options and return modified arguments for brms   configure_opts <- nlist(sort_data, silent, backend, parallel = dots$parallel,                           cores = dots$cores)   opts <- configure_options(configure_opts)   dots$parallel <- NULL    # check model, formula and data, and transform data if necessary   user_formula <- formula   model <- check_model(model, data, formula)   data <- check_data(model, data, formula)   formula <- check_formula(model, data, formula)    # generate the model specification to pass to brms later   config_args <- configure_model(model, data, formula)    # configure the default prior and combine with user-specified prior   prior <- configure_prior(model, data, config_args$formula, prior)    # estimate the model   fit_args <- combine_args(nlist(config_args, opts, dots, prior))   fit <- call_brm(fit_args)    # model post-processing   fit <- postprocess_brm(model, fit, fit_args = fit_args, user_formula = user_formula,                          configure_opts = configure_opts)    # save the fitted model object if !is.null   save_bmmfit(fit, file, compress = file_compress) }

title: Easy and Accessible Bayesian Measurement Models Using brms
text: arrive data task, models organized. lists generated package, show models version page built . Continuous reproduction. Participants reproduce color, orientation another continuous feature, response error dependent variable. See continuous reproduction article. imm(): Interference measurement model Oberauer Lin (2017) mixture2p(): Two-parameter mixture model Zhang Luck (2008) mixture3p(): Three-parameter mixture model Bays et al (2009) sdm(): Signal Discrimination Model (SDM) Oberauer (2023) Categorical recall n-AFC decisions. Participants choose one response set categories (n-alternative forced choice), example correct item, item another position, item studied. See M3 article. m3(): Multinomial / Memory Measurement Model Detection, recognition confidence judgments. Participants decide whether signal present item studied, rate confidence, give Remember/Know judgments, pick target among several alternatives, rank alternatives. One signal detection model per response format, fit response counts per participant condition. See signal detection article , dual-process meta-d′ versions sdt_rating() Remember/Know model sdt_cdp(), dual-process meta-d′ article. Get started page table response formats noise distributions model offers. sdt_cdp(): Continuous Dual-Process Signal Detection Theory (CDP) sdt_mafc(): Signal Detection Theory (m-AFC) sdt_ranking(): Signal Detection Theory (Ranking) sdt_rating(): Signal Detection Theory (Confidence Rating) sdt_yn(): Signal Detection Theory (Yes/) Choices response times. Participants choose two options response time recorded, either every trial means variances per condition. See DDM, censored shifted Wald, EZ-diffusion response time contamination articles. cswald(): Censored-Shifted Wald Model ddm(): Diffusion Decision Model ezdm(): EZ-Diffusion Model  supported_models() prints list R, ?modelname (example ?imm) documents data model expects parameters mean.

title: Distribution functions for the Signal Discrimination Model (SDM) — SDMdist
text: Parametrization See online article details parameterization. Oberauer (2023) introduced SDM bessel parametrization. sqrtexp parametrization default bmm package numerical stability efficiency. two parametrizations related functions c_bessel2sqrtexp() c_sqrtexp2bessel(). cumulative distribution function Since responses circle, cumulative distribution function requires choose lower bound integration. default \(-\pi\), brms::pvon_mises() function can choose value argument lower_bound psdm. Another useful choice mean response distribution minus \(\pi\), e.g. lower_bound = mu-pi. default circular::pvonmises(), ensures 50% cumulative probability mass mean response distribution.

title: Utility functions for Signal Detection Theory — SDTdist
code: sdt_d(   hit_rate,   fa_rate,   dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic") )  sdt_criterion(   hit_rate,   fa_rate,   dist = c("normal", "gumbel_min", "gumbel_max", "logistic") )

title: Utility functions for Signal Detection Theory — SDTdist
text: hit_rate Numeric. Proportion hits (P("old" | signal)). fa_rate Numeric. Proportion false alarms (P("old" | noise)). dist Character. distribution assumed latent evidence, given cumulative distribution function: "normal" (default): Gaussian, \(\Phi(x)\) "gumbel_min": smallest extreme value, \(1 - \exp(-\exp(x))\) (complementary log-log distribution) "gumbel_max": largest extreme value, \(\exp(-\exp(-x))\) (log-log distribution, evd::pgumbel) "logistic": \(1 / (1 + \exp(-x))\)

title: Utility functions for Signal Detection Theory — SDTdist
text: sdt_d returns distance signal noise distributions latent evidence axis, obtained inverting decision rule "respond old evidence exceeds criterion": \(Q(1 - FA) - Q(1 - H)\), \(Q\) quantile function dist. dist = "normal" reduces familiar \(d' = \Phi^{-1}(H) - \Phi^{-1}(FA)\). one operating point implies equal variance, matches d parameter sdt_yn() whenever sdratio default. sdt_criterion returns criterion (response bias) centred, noise-standardized evidence axis used sdt_yn(), noise signal distributions sit -d'/2 +d'/2: \((Q(1 - FA) + Q(1 - H)) / 2\). dist = "normal" reduces familiar \(-(\Phi^{-1}(H) + \Phi^{-1}(FA)) / 2\).

title: Utility functions for Signal Detection Theory — SDTdist
text: Green, D. M., & Swets, J. . (1966). Signal detection theory psychophysics. Wiley.

title: Utility functions for Signal Detection Theory — SDTdist
code: # Compute d from hit and false alarm rates (Gaussian SDT) sdt_d(hit_rate = 0.8, fa_rate = 0.2, dist = "normal") #> [1] 1.683242  # The extreme-value analogue sdt_d(hit_rate = 0.75, fa_rate = 0.25, dist = "gumbel_min") #> [1] 1.572534 # Compute criterion from hit and false alarm rates sdt_criterion(hit_rate = 0.8, fa_rate = 0.2, dist = "normal") #> [1] 0

what: Area under the ROC curve from a fitted SDT model — auc_sdt
title: Area under the ROC curve from a fitted SDT model — auc_sdt
text: Computes posterior area ROC curve (AUC). Gaussian Gumbel (min max) equal-variance binary SDT AUC available closed form d draws; otherwise obtained trapezoidal integration model-implied curve (rating fits, curve swept posterior d sdratio, lifted Ro/Rn version = "dpsdt", AUC area predicted mixture ROC \(\Phi(d/\sqrt{2})\); version = "metad" type-1 curve). returned AUC always area full curve, trapezoid discrete operating points K-1 rating thresholds; binary multi-criteria fits one value per curve.

title: Area under the ROC curve from a fitted SDT model — auc_sdt
text: fit bmmfit object returned bmm() SDT model. conditions Optional data frame predictor values evaluate model. Column names must match predictor variables used formula. NULL (default), unique predictor combinations derived data. probs Numeric vector length 2. Quantiles credible interval (default c(0.025, 0.975)). criterion_points Optional. Control binary multi-criteria behaviour. NULL (default) auto-detects predictors vary criterion (d/sdratio) treats levels operating points one curve. Pass character vector column names force classification, FALSE disable (one separate curve per predictor combination). Ignored rating models. ... Additional arguments passed brms::posterior_linpred(), draw_ids use subset posterior draws. ndraws refused: parameter drawn call, random subsets match across parameters.

title: Area under the ROC curve from a fitted SDT model — auc_sdt

title: Area under the ROC curve from a fitted SDT model — auc_sdt
text: closed form used sdratio fixed 0, d (\(d_a\)) equals \(d'\); every fit sdratio estimated fixed away 0 takes numerical route, AUC invariant sensitivity parameterization. Analytical formulas (equal variance, \(d_a = d'\)): normal EV-SDT \(AUC = \Phi(d'/\sqrt{2})\); Gumbel-min Gumbel-max EV-SDT \(AUC = \mathrm{logistic}(g')\).

code: if (FALSE) { # isTRUE(Sys.getenv("BMM_EXAMPLES")) configure_model.mixture3p <- function(model, data, formula) {   # retrieve arguments from the data check   max_set_size <- attr(data, "max_set_size")   lure_idx <- attr(data, "lure_idx_vars")   nt_features <- model$other_vars$nt_features   set_size_var <- model$other_vars$set_size    # construct initial brms formula   formula <- bmf2bf(model, formula) +     brms::lf(kappa2 ~ 1) +     brms::lf(mu2 ~ 1) +     brms::nlf(theta1 ~ thetat) +     brms::nlf(kappa1 ~ kappa)    # additional internal terms for the mixture model formula   kappa_nts <- paste0("kappa", 3:(max_set_size + 1))   theta_nts <- paste0("theta", 3:(max_set_size + 1))   mu_nts <- paste0("mu", 3:(max_set_size + 1))    for (i in 1:(max_set_size - 1)) {     formula <- formula +       glue_nlf("{kappa_nts[i]} ~ kappa") +       glue_nlf(         "{theta_nts[i]} ~ {lure_idx[i]} * (thetant + log(inv_ss)) + ",         "(1 - {lure_idx[i]}) * (-100)"       ) +       glue_nlf("{mu_nts[i]} ~ {nt_features[i]}")   }    # define mixture family   vm_list <- lapply(1:(max_set_size + 1), function(x) brms::von_mises(link = "identity"))   vm_list$order <- "none"   formula$family <- brms::do_call(brms::mixture, vm_list)    nlist(formula, data) } }

code: if (FALSE) { # isTRUE(Sys.getenv("BMM_EXAMPLES")) configure_prior.mixture3p <- function(model, data, formula, user_prior, ...) {   # if there is set_size 1 in the data, set constant prior over thetant for set_size1   prior <- brms::empty_prior()   set_size_var <- model$other_vars$set_size   prior_cond <- any(data$ss_numeric == 1) && !is.numeric(data[[set_size_var]])    thetant_preds <- rhs_vars(formula$pforms$thetant)   if (prior_cond && set_size_var %in% thetant_preds) {     prior <- prior + brms::prior_("constant(-100)",       class = "b",       coef = paste0(set_size_var, 1),       nlpar = "thetant"     )   }   # check if there is a random effect on theetant that include set_size as predictor   bterms <- brms::brmsterms(formula$pforms$thetant)   re_terms <- bterms$dpars$mu$re   if (!is.null(re_terms)) {     for (i in 1:nrow(re_terms)) {       group <- re_terms$group[[i]]       form <- re_terms$form[[i]]       thetant_preds <- rhs_vars(form)        if (prior_cond && set_size_var %in% thetant_preds) {         prior <- prior + brms::prior_("constant(1e-8)",           class = "sd",           coef = paste0(set_size_var, 1),           group = group,           nlpar = "thetant"         )       }     }   }    prior } }

title: Censored-Shifted Wald Model — cswald
text: rt name variable dataset containing response times. Response times coded seconds (milliseconds). response name variable dataset containing response/decision. Responses coded 0 (lower boundary) 1 (upper boundary). Alternatively, character values "lower" "upper" logical values (FALSE/TRUE) accepted converted automatically. links named list link functions model parameters. Available parameters depend version: "simple" drift, bound, ndt, s; "crisk" additionally zr. Default links "log" parameters "logit" zr. positive parameters, "softplus" available alternative "log" grows linearly large values avoids numerical blow-exp(). name parameter model error, link allows values default link excludes (e.g. "identity" positive parameter) warning. version character string specifying version cswald model use. Options : "simple" (default): standard censored shifted Wald model, treats error responses censored correct responses. Best suited tasks errors (<20%). Note: bound parameter simple version represents distance starting point correct boundary, half total boundary separation diffusion model (assuming unbiased starting point). convert full boundary separation (DDM crisk), multiply 2. "crisk": competing risks version, models response types arising racing accumulators toward opposite boundaries. Better suited tasks substantial error rates. bound parameter represents total boundary separation, consistent diffusion model parameterization. details, see Miller et al. (2017). ... Additional arguments passed internally (testing purposes).

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Minimal parameter recovery example with 3-parameter EZDM  # Simulate data from known parameters set.seed(123) sim_data <- rezdm(   n = 10,   n_trials = 100,   drift = 2,   bound = 1.5,   ndt = 0.3,   version = "3par" )  # Add subject ID sim_data$id <- 1:10  # Specify model model <- ezdm(   mean_rt = "mean_rt",   var_rt = "var_rt",   n_upper = "n_upper",   n_trials = "n_trials",   version = "3par" )  # Specify formula with random effects formula <- bmf(   drift ~ 1 + (1 | id),   bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),   ndt ~ 1 )  # Fit model (using cmdstanr backend) fit <- bmm(   formula = formula,   data = sim_data,   model = model,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4,   chains = 4,   iter = 2000,   warmup = 1000 )  # Check parameter recovery summary(fit)  # Extract population-level effects # True values: drift = 2, bound = 1.5, ndt = 0.3 (on log scale for drift/bound) exp(brms::fixef(fit)) } # }

title: Three-parameter mixture model by Bays et al (2009). — mixture3p
text: Domain: Visual working memory Task: Continuous reproduction Name: Three-parameter mixture model Bays et al (2009). Citation: Bays, P. M., Catalao, R. F. G., & Husain, M. (2009). precision visual working memory set allocation shared resource. Journal Vision, 9(10), 1-11 Requirements: response vairable radians represent angular error relative target non-target features radians centered relative target Parameters: mu1: Location parameter von Mises distribution memory responses (radians). Fixed internally 0 default. kappa: Concentration parameter von Mises distribution thetat: Mixture weight target responses thetant: Mixture weight non-target responses Fixed parameters: mu1 = 0 mu2 = 0 kappa2 = -100 Default parameter links: mu1 = tan_half; kappa = log; thetat = softmax; thetant = softmax Default priors: mu1: main: normal(0, 0.5) effects: normal(0, 0.25) sd: exponential(4) kappa: main: normal(2, 1) effects: normal(0, 1) sd: exponential(1) thetat: main: logistic(0, 1) effects: normal(0, 2.5) sd: exponential(1) thetant: main: logistic(0, 1) effects: normal(0, 2.5) sd: exponential(1)

title: Three-parameter mixture model by Bays et al (2009). — mixture3p
code: if (FALSE) { # isTRUE(Sys.getenv("BMM_EXAMPLES")) # generate artificial data from the Bays et al (2009) 3-parameter mixture model dat <- data.frame(   y = rmixture3p(n = 2000, mu = c(0, 1, -1.5, 2)),   nt1_loc = 1,   nt2_loc = -1.5,   nt3_loc = 2 )  # define formula ff <- bmmformula(   kappa ~ 1,   thetat ~ 1,   thetant ~ 1 )  # specify the 3-parameter model with explicit column names for non-target features model1 <- mixture3p(resp_error = "y", nt_features = paste0("nt", 1:3, "_loc"), set_size = 4)  # fit the model fit <- bmm(   formula = ff,   data = dat,   model = model1,   cores = 4,   iter = 500,   backend = "cmdstanr" )  # alternatively specify the 3-parameter model with a regular expression to match non-target features # this is equivalent to the previous call, but more concise model2 <- mixture3p(resp_error = "y", nt_features = "nt.*_loc", set_size = 4, regex = TRUE)  # fit the model fit <- bmm(   formula = ff,   data = dat,   model = model2,   cores = 4,   iter = 500,   backend = "cmdstanr" ) }

title: Continuous Dual-Process Signal Detection Theory Model — sdt_cdp
text: Domain: Recognition Memory Task: Old/New Recognition Remember/Know Judgments Name: Continuous Dual-Process Signal Detection Theory (CDP) Citation: Wixted, J. T., & Mickes, L. Must coded 0 (noise/new) 1 (signal/old). dist distribution assumed latent evidence, given cumulative distribution function. One : "normal" (default): Gaussian SDT, \(\Phi(x)\) "gumbel_min": smallest-extreme-value SDT, \(1 - \exp(-\exp(x))\) (complementary log-log) "gumbel_max": largest-extreme-value SDT, \(\exp(-\exp(-x))\) (log-log, evd::pgumbel) "logistic": logistic SDT, \(1 / (1 + \exp(-x))\) threshold_type Character. Threshold parameterization: "parsimonious" (default): 2 parameters (criterion + spacing). Thresholds follow logit-spaced canonical positions (Selker et al., 2019). "equidistant": 2 parameters (criterion + spacing). Thresholds equally spaced, exp(spacing) apart. "log_distance": K-2 parameters. delta<> log width interval thresholds + 1, intervals free ordering guaranteed (Paulewicz & Blaut, 2022). "log_ratio": K-2 parameters (Paulewicz & Blaut, 2022; odd-K form bmm's). One interval spread, exp(delta): even K interval just criterion, odd K middle category. first interval side (even K) side (odd K) ratio times spread, every interval ratio times first interval side. deltas therefore exchangeable; model$parameters names role . "softmax": K-2 parameters. shared spacing parameter sets mean interval width, exp(spacing), K-3 delta parameters share total width intervals softmax (delta log ratio interval last one). version Character. latent-process version rating model. One "standard" (default, single familiarity SDT process), "dpsdt" (dual-process SDT recollection parameters Ro/Rn), "metad" (meta-d' metacognitive efficiency parameter logmratio, log M-ratio). three use confidence-rating response interface. text: Meta-d' (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012): type-2 metacognitive sensitivity governs confidence-threshold placement, total "old"/"new" response rates held type-1 d implies. Rather estimating meta-d' directly, model estimates logmratio, log M-ratio \(\log(\mathrm{meta\text{-}d'}/d')\), recovers meta-d' exp(logmratio) * d. M-ratio field-standard measure metacognitive efficiency (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012; Fleming, 2017): estimating log scale keeps meta-d' positive, regularizes toward d, anchors ideal point (meta-d' = d, perfect metacognition) logmratio = 0, recovers standard. Type-1 type-2 sensitivity share one scale (\(d'\), \(d_a\) sdratio estimated), M-ratio unaffected sdratio. type-1 boundary criterion, middle threshold, version needs even number rating categories: odd number middle category straddles boundary (see "criterion sits"). type-1 criterion held location meta-d' space type-1 model, HMeta-d toolbox's model equations (Fleming, 2017, Appendix). Maximum-likelihood meta-d' instead constrains meta-c' = c' (Maniscalco & Lau, 2014), estimates differ bmm's criterion far midpoint. Extract M-ratio posterior mratio(). title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: Uses Bayesian Beta-Binomial conjugate analysis test whether fast flagged contaminants show random guessing (~50% accuracy 2AFC). test computes posterior distribution proportion "upper" responses uses Savage-Dickey Bayes Factor quantify evidence guessing hypothesis.

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
code: validate_fast_guesses(   contam_flag,   rt_data,   response,   threshold_type = c("quantile", "absolute"),   rt_threshold = 0.25,   prior_alpha = 1,   prior_beta = 1,   guess_prob = 0.5,   credible_mass = 0.95 )

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: contam_flag Logical vector indicating trials flagged contaminants rt_data Numeric vector reaction times (seconds) response Response data format accepted .convert_response_to_upper() (numeric 0/1, logical, character, factor) threshold_type Character. interpret rt_threshold: "quantile" (default): Use rt_threshold quantile (0-1) "absolute": Use rt_threshold absolute RT seconds rt_threshold Numeric. Threshold defining "fast" trials. Interpretation depends threshold_type: threshold_type = "quantile" (default): Quantile RT distribution (e.g., 0.25 = 25th percentile). Default 0.25. threshold_type = "absolute": Absolute RT value seconds (e.g., 0.25 = 250ms). prior_alpha, prior_beta Numeric. Parameters Beta prior distribution. Default 1,1 gives uniform prior. Values > 1 express prior belief response proportions. guess_prob Numeric. Null hypothesis value guessing probability. Default 0.5 (equal probability upper/lower responses). credible_mass Numeric. Probability mass Highest Density Interval. Default 0.95 95% HDI. Common alternatives: 0.90, 0.99.

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: List components: method: "bayesian" prop_upper: Observed proportion upper responses hdi_lower, hdi_upper: 95% Highest Density Interval bounds bf_01: Bayes Factor H0 (guessing) vs H1 (non-random) guess_in_hdi: Logical, whether guess_prob HDI bf_evidence: Character, evidence category Jeffreys scale posterior_alpha, posterior_beta: Posterior Beta parameters n_tested: Number fast flagged trials tested rt_threshold: Actual RT threshold value used (seconds) threshold_type: Type threshold used ("quantile" "absolute") credible_mass: Credible mass used HDI computation mean_rt_tested: Mean RT tested trials

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: function performs Bayesian test using Beta-Binomial conjugate prior-posterior relationship. Beta(alpha, beta) prior observing n_upper "upper" responses n_tested trials, posterior : Beta(alpha + n_upper, beta + n_lower) Savage-Dickey Bayes Factor compares posterior prior densities null hypothesis value (default 0.5): BF_01 = posterior_density(guess_prob) / prior_density(guess_prob) Evidence categories follow Jeffreys (1961) scale: BF > 10: Strong evidence guessing BF > 3: Moderate evidence guessing BF > 1: Anecdotal evidence guessing BF < 1/3: Moderate evidence guessing BF < 1/10: Strong evidence guessing Note: function can used standalone validation step obtaining contamination probabilities flag_contaminant_rts().

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: Jeffreys, H. (1961). Theory Probability (3rd ed.). Oxford University Press.

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Simulate data with random guessing on fast trials set.seed(123) n <- 100 rt <- c(runif(20, 0.15, 0.30), rgamma(80, 5, 10)) response <- c(rbinom(20, 1, 0.5), rbinom(80, 1, 0.7)) contam_flag <- rt < 0.35  # Test using quantile threshold (default, adaptive) result1 <- validate_fast_guesses(   contam_flag = contam_flag,   rt_data = rt,   response = response,   threshold_type = "quantile",   rt_threshold = 0.30 # 30th percentile )  # Test using absolute threshold (fixed RT) result2 <- validate_fast_guesses(   contam_flag = contam_flag,   rt_data = rt,   response = response,   threshold_type = "absolute",   rt_threshold = 0.30 # 300ms )  print(result1$bf_01) # Bayes Factor print(result1$bf_evidence) # Evidence category print(result1$guess_in_hdi) # Is 0.5 in 95% HDI? print(result1$threshold_type) # "quantile" } # }

title: bmm (development version)
text: Add Yes/Signal Detection Theory (sdt_yn) detection old/new recognition tasks aggregated response counts. estimates sensitivity (d) response bias (criterion), optionally unequal-variance ratio (sdratio). Also adds dsdt_yn(), rsdt_yn(), sdt_d() sdt_criterion(). See ?sdt_yn parameters, links, default priors designs identify sdratio. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn Add m-Alternative Forced Choice Signal Detection Theory (sdt_mafc) accuracy-m-AFC tasks, one m alternatives carries signal (DeCarlo, 2012). estimates sensitivity (d) response counts bias parameter. m may constant name data column, trials different numbers alternatives can fit jointly. Also adds dsdt_mafc() rsdt_mafc(). See ?sdt_mafc parameters, noise distributions, default priors d relates sensitivity sdt_yn() reports. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn Add Ranking Signal Detection Theory (sdt_ranking) tasks observers rank m items, one studied target, strongly recognise (Meyer-Grant et al., 2026). estimates sensitivity (d) target’s rank counts, Gumbel ("gumbel_min") Gaussian ("normal") noise. m may constant name data column, trials different set sizes can fit jointly. Also adds dsdt_ranking() rsdt_ranking(). See ?sdt_ranking parameters, response format default priors. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn Add Confidence Rating Signal Detection Theory (sdt_rating) old/new recognition detection tasks ordered confidence ratings, aggregated counts per rating category. estimates sensitivity (d), response bias (criterion) confidence thresholds, optionally unequal-variance ratio (sdratio); threshold_type chooses thresholds parameterized. Also adds dsdt_rating() rsdt_rating(). See ?sdt_rating parameters, threshold types, default priors d relates sensitivity sdt_yn() reports. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn Add two versions sdt_rating(), selected version: "dpsdt", dual-process model (Yonelinas, 1994) recollection old items (Ro) recall--reject new items (Rn; Yonelinas, 2024), "metad", meta-d’ model, estimates metacognitive efficiency log M-ratio logmratio (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012). reduce standard model extra parameters . Also adds mratio(), dsdt_dpsdt(), rsdt_dpsdt(), dsdt_metad() rsdt_metad(). See ?sdt_rating. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn Add Continuous Dual-Process Signal Detection Theory (sdt_cdp) old/new recognition Remember/Know judgments (Wixted & Mickes, 2010). estimates familiarity (dfam) recollection (drec) sensitivity, old/new criterion, confidence thresholds Remember criterion (rcrit) aggregated response counts; recollection SD (sigmar), familiarity-recollection correlation (rho) Know/Guess criterion (kcrit) can freed formula. Also adds aggregate_sdt_cdp_data(), dsdt_cdp() rsdt_cdp(). See ?sdt_cdp parameters, response format drec relates sensitivity sdt_yn() reports. Thanks @GidonFrischkorn

title: bmm 1.3.0
text: Add Diffusion Decision Model (ddm) speeded decision-making tasks trial-level RT response data. model estimates drift rate, boundary separation, non-decision time, (optionally) relative starting point. Includes distribution functions dddm() rddm() (#280). Add EZ-Diffusion Model (ezdm) speeded decision-making tasks. model estimates drift rate, boundary separation, non-decision time aggregated summary statistics (mean RT, variance RT, accuracy) using closed-form equations derived Wagenmakers et al. (2007). Supports 3-parameter (symmetric starting point) 4-parameter (asymmetric starting point) versions based Srivastava et al. (2016). Implements Bayesian hierarchical estimation following Chavez & Vandekerckhove (2025). Includes distribution functions dezdm() rezdm() (#281). Add Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald) choice reaction time tasks two response boundaries. model estimates drift rate, boundary separation, non-decision time trial-level RT response data. Implements two versions: simple (treats errors censored correct responses, appropriate high-accuracy tasks) crisk (competing risks version separate accumulators response, suitable balanced accuracy). Includes distribution functions dcswald(), pcswald(), qcswald(), rcswald(). Thanks @GidonFrischkorn

New S3 methods emmeans support bmmfit objects. Users can now call emmeans(fit, ~ condition, dpar = "kappa") bmmodel (#323). New pp_check() method multinomial models (e.g., m3). Since brms::pp_check() support multinomial family, bmm now provides custom method compares observed predicted response proportions ppc_bars style bayesplot. method supports faceting experimental conditions via group, configurable credible intervals via probs, population-level predictions via re_formula = NA. non-multinomial models, pp_check() delegates brms::pp_check() auto-selects grouped plot variant group specified (#324). New function parameters() lists parameters bmmodel bmmfit object descriptions, link functions, fixed values (#329). New function extract_stan_blocks() extracts individual program blocks (functions, data, parameters, etc.) compiled Stan code (#286). New function extract_parameter_dimensions() extracts parameter names, dimensions, types Stan parameters block. New functions ezdm_summary_stats() adjust_ezdm_accuracy() compute pre-process summary statistics trial-level RT data EZ-Diffusion Model (#291). New functions flag_contaminant_rts() validate_fast_guesses() trial-level contamination detection RT data. Identifies fast guesses attention lapses using mixture modeling provides Bayesian validation fast guess assumptions (#307).
